newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Eurotunnel up on licence news.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Eurotunnel up on licence news.

text.p: Eurotunnel shares jumped on Wednesday on news its operating licence may be extended -- but a group of disgruntled investors said it was unimpressed by the deal and would fight the group's crucial refinancing plan.
The French Bourse briefly suspended the shares when they rose by over 20 percent in the morning and the Channel Tunnel operator's stock kept outperforming the market later on.
At 1310 GMT, Eurotunnel was up eight percent at 7.45 francs while the blue-chip index was down 1.35 percent.
"It's a good deal as far as investor confidence is concerned because it makes the chance of a 'yes' vote (by investors for the debt plan) much higher," said analyst Richard Hannah at UBS.
But he added the licence extension to at least 99 years did not have a big financial impact because it was the first few years that really counted.
"If it survives in 10 years, it will survive in the long term as well."

The French finance minstry said on Tuesday that France and Britain were ready to extend Eurotunnel SA/Plc's concession to at least 99 years from the current 65-year licence, which runs out in 2052. Conditions included acceptance by Eurotunnel shareholders of the 70 billion francs ($12 billion) debt plan and payment of 25 percent of Eurotunnel profits from 2052.
But a small group of mainly French shareholders, Adacte, said on Wednesday the licence extension did not meet a basic demand, that banks cancel 40 percent of loans to Eurotunnel.

"We think the only way for Eurotunnel to be viable is that the banks abandon part of the debt," spokeswoman Emmanuelle Bobin said. Without a write-off, debt service problems would be postponed for a few years before another debt restructuring.

In any future debt deal, Adacte believes shareholders will be further diluted to a quarter of the capital from the 54.5 percent proposed in the current deal. "They will lose their voice, it will be too late," Bobin said.
Adacte has gathered proxy votes for around two million shares and expects proxies for at least 10 million for a shareholders' meeting next week which will vote on the deal.
It believes that, with the help of proxies for institutional investors held by lawyer Sophie L'Helias, the deal can be blocked, forcing bankers to give up some of their loans.

Adacte rejected executive Eurotunnel chairman Patrick Ponsolle's recent warnings that the company would go bankrupt if investors threw out the debt restructuring. "They will appoint someone else to clean up the mess," Bobin said.

The investor resistance movement suffered a setback on Monday when U.S. fund Northern Cross Investments, which holds three percent of Eurotunnel's stock, instructed L'Helias to vote in favour of the restructuring, reversing its earlier position.

However, that change of heart did not change the view of other investors represented by L'Helias, who will vote against the debt deal. They are calling for 25 percent debt forgiveness and a cancellation of the "substitution clause" which allows banks to take over the Tunnel. L'Helias's office was not immediately available to say how many shares it now represented.
Eurotunnel has a total of just under 920 million shares.

Christian Cambier of the Eurotunnel Shareholders Association, which represents mainly professional class investors, welcomed the licence extension and said the 25 percent profit share for the governments was acceptable.

"The 99 years give a better visibility," he said, adding it also meant Eurotunnel did not need to put money into reserves to bid for a renewal of its licence when the current concession expires in 2052 as previously planned.
"Twenty-five percent for the government means 75 for the shareholders," he said. Under the debt deal, all the interest would have been paid off by 2034.
Eurotunnel needs two thirds consent from French shareholders and 75 percent from British investors. The shareholders meeting has been called for July 10.
